plan: SAT R&W batch 75: 20 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000704..000723 (8 SEC: Sacagawea who, Bayard Rustin finite verb, Fannie Lou Hamer colon, Shirley Chisholm past perfect, Jim Thorpe however, Roberto Clemente modifier, Mendel findings agreement, Copernicus "the number of"; Maria Tallchief and lotus WIC; transistor purpose; magpie mirror structure; Kohda/Gallup cleaner wrasse cross-text; orca grandmother inference; termite mound data; spider silk evidence; kingfisher bullet train central idea; Wilma Mankiller and Argentine ant transitions; Althea Gibson synthesis). Topics checked against both workstreams. Plus S074-08, S074-18, S074-19, S074-20 (revision 2) on previously unbanked passages. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Across the continent
passages.text: Sacagawea, a Lemhi Shoshone woman ______ traveled with the Lewis and Clark expedition from 1805 to 1806, helped the explorers communicate with Shoshone people and carried her infant son for much of the journey.

passages.title: Planning a march
passages.text: Bayard Rustin, the chief organizer of the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, ______ the logistics for a gathering of about 250,000 people in roughly two months, arranging everything from buses and trains to drinking water and first-aid stations.

passages.title: Sick and tired
passages.text: The civil rights activist Fannie Lou Hamer summed up her frustration in a phrase that became ______ "I am sick and tired of being sick and tired."

passages.title: Unbought and unbossed
passages.text: In 1972, Shirley Chisholm, who four years earlier ______ the first Black woman elected to the U.S. Congress, became the first Black candidate to seek a major party's nomination for president.

passages.title: Medals restored
passages.text: At the 1912 Olympic Games in Stockholm, Jim Thorpe won gold medals in both the pentathlon and the decathlon. The next ______ his medals were taken away because he had earlier been paid to play minor-league baseball.

passages.title: A final journey
passages.text: Roberto Clemente spent eighteen seasons with the Pittsburgh Pirates and finished his career with exactly 3,000 hits. On December 31, 1972, he died in a plane crash while flying relief supplies to earthquake survivors in Nicaragua. Honored the following year in a special election, ______

passages.title: Peas and patterns
passages.text: Working in the garden of his monastery in what is now the Czech Republic, Gregor Mendel bred thousands of pea plants and tracked how traits such as seed color passed from one generation to the next. His findings, published in 1866, ______ largely overlooked until 1900, when other scientists independently reached similar conclusions.

passages.title: Counting the copies
passages.text: In 1543, Nicolaus Copernicus published a book arguing that Earth and the other planets travel around the Sun. Historian Owen Gingerich spent decades tracking down surviving copies of its first two editions, and he found that the number of copies that survive ______ surprisingly large: about 600.

passages.title: The Firebird
passages.text: In 1949, the Osage ballerina Maria Tallchief danced the title role in George Balanchine's version of The Firebird. Critics praised the ______ of her performance, marveling at the speed and exactness with which she executed the role's demanding steps.

passages.title: Self-cleaning leaves
passages.text: The leaves of the sacred lotus stay remarkably clean even though the plant grows in muddy water. The leaves are strongly ______: water landing on them forms nearly spherical beads that roll off, picking up particles of dirt as they go.

passages.title: A small switch
passages.text: Early electronic devices relied on vacuum tubes, which were bulky, fragile, and power-hungry. In December 1947, physicists John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, working in William Shockley's group at Bell Labs, demonstrated the first working transistor, a device that could amplify and switch electrical signals as vacuum tubes did. Transistors were far smaller and used much less power, and they made portable radios and, later, computers practical. Today a single smartphone chip contains billions of them.

passages.title: A bird and a mirror
passages.text: Scientists once thought that only a few mammals, such as great apes, could recognize themselves in a mirror. In a 2008 study, researchers placed a small colored mark on the throat feathers of Eurasian magpies, where the birds could see it only in a mirror. Several magpies tried repeatedly to remove the mark when they saw their reflection but not when the mark was invisible or no mirror was present. The study became the first widely cited evidence of mirror self-recognition in a non-mammal.

passages.title: Can a fish know itself?
passages.text:
Text 1
In a 2019 study, biologist Masanori Kohda and colleagues placed a colored mark on the throats of cleaner wrasses, small fish that eat parasites off larger fish. After seeing themselves in a mirror, many of the fish scraped their throats against the bottom of the tank. Kohda's team concluded that the fish had passed the mirror test, which is often treated as evidence of self-recognition.

Text 2
Psychologist Gordon Gallup, who developed the mirror test in 1970, questioned that conclusion. He argued that cleaner wrasses spend their lives looking for marks resembling parasites on other fish, so a fish scraping at such a mark after seeing one in a mirror may be responding to a parasite-like spot rather than recognizing itself.

passages.title: Grandmothers in the lead
passages.text: Resident killer whales off the Pacific coast of North America live in family groups, and some females survive for decades after they stop reproducing. In a 2015 study, researchers analyzing years of video found that these older females often led their groups while traveling, and that they led most often in years when salmon, the whales' main food, was scarce. This finding suggests that ______

passages.title: Inside a termite mound
passages.text:
A student recorded temperatures inside and outside a large termite mound at three times on a summer day.
6 a.m.: outside 20°C; inside 29°C
2 p.m.: outside 35°C; inside 31°C
10 p.m.: outside 22°C; inside 30°C
The student claims that the temperature inside the mound stayed much more stable than the temperature outside it.

passages.title: Strong as silk
passages.text: Spider dragline silk is, for its weight, stronger than steel. Researchers hypothesize that much of this strength comes from tiny crystalline regions within the silk's proteins, which are linked by more flexible, disordered regions.

passages.title: A train like a bird
passages.text: When Japan's bullet trains entered tunnels at high speed, they pushed air ahead of them, and when the trains exited, the compressed air burst out with a loud boom that disturbed nearby residents. Eiji Nakatsu, an engineer and birdwatcher, noticed that kingfishers dive into water with barely a splash. His team redesigned the front of the 500 Series train with a long, tapered nose modeled on the kingfisher's beak. The new train was quieter in tunnels, and it also ran faster while using less electricity.

passages.title: Chief of the Cherokee Nation
passages.text: Wilma Mankiller became principal chief of the Cherokee Nation in 1985, when her predecessor resigned to take a position in the federal government. ______ she won election to the office in her own right in 1987, and voters reelected her in 1991 by a wide margin.

passages.title: An empire of ants
passages.text: Argentine ants from different nests usually treat one another as nestmates rather than as rivals, and they rarely fight. ______ in parts of southern Europe, connected nests of these ants form a single "supercolony" that stretches for roughly 6,000 kilometers along the coast.

passages.title: Notes on a champion
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In 1950, Althea Gibson became the first Black player to compete at the U.S. National Championships in tennis.
- In 1956, she won the French Championships, becoming the first Black player to win a Grand Slam title.
- She won both Wimbledon and the U.S. Nationals in 1957 and 1958.
- In 1964, she became the first Black woman to join the Ladies Professional Golf Association (LPGA) tour.

passages.title: Rumbles below hearing
passages.text: In the 1980s, the biologist Katy Payne discovered that elephants communicate in part through ______ low-pitched rumbles below the range of human hearing that can travel several kilometers.

passages.title: Learning the new machines
passages.text: In the 1950s, as the laboratory at Langley, Virginia, began relying on electronic computers, many of the human "computers" who did calculations by hand worried about their jobs. Dorothy Vaughan, a mathematician who had supervised a group of Black women computers there, saw that the machines were the future. ______ she taught herself the programming language FORTRAN and became an expert programmer.

passages.title: A petition to learn
passages.text: Mary Jackson, a mathematician at the Langley laboratory of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (the agency that later became NASA), wanted to become an engineer, but some of the courses she needed were taught at a high school in Hampton, Virginia, that was then open only to white students. ______ she petitioned the city for permission to attend. The request was granted, and in 1958 she became NASA's first Black female engineer.

passages.title: Notes on a mathematician
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Gladys West began working as a mathematician at the Naval Surface Warfare Center in Dahlgren, Virginia, in 1956.
- She programmed computers to build an extremely precise mathematical model of Earth's shape using satellite data.
- Models like hers are needed for the Global Positioning System (GPS) to calculate locations accurately.
- Many people now use GPS every day on their phones.
- In 2018, she was inducted into the U.S. Air Force Space and Missile Pioneers Hall of Fame.

candidates.subskill: Relative pronoun in an appositive clause
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: helped the explorers communicate with Shoshone people
candidates.explanation: "Who traveled with the Lewis and Clark expedition" describes the woman; "who" is the subject of "traveled."

A.rationale: The pronoun is the subject of "traveled," so the subject form is needed.

C.rationale: "She" creates a second subject inside the appositive and leaves the clause unconnected.

hints: Is the pronoun the subject or the object of "traveled"?

strategy.explanation: Find the verb the pronoun goes with.

candidates.remember: Use "who" as the subject of a relative clause.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: arranging everything from buses and trains to drinking water
candidates.explanation: The subject "Bayard Rustin" needs a main verb; "coordinated" supplies it.

A.rationale: "Coordinating" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

B.rationale: "Who coordinated" turns the predicate into a clause, leaving no main verb.

C.rationale: "Having coordinated" is a participle, so the sentence would lack a main verb.

hints: What is the main verb of the sentence?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence without the appositive.

candidates.remember: Every sentence needs a finite main verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: summed up her frustration in a phrase
candidates.explanation: A colon after the complete clause correctly introduces the quotation that the clause announces.

B.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, not a quotation standing alone.

C.rationale: "It was" creates a comma splice between two independent clauses.

D.rationale: "That" cannot introduce a direct quotation here.

hints: Does the clause before the blank announce what comes after it?

strategy.explanation: Check what each mark can introduce.

candidates.remember: A colon can introduce a quotation after a complete clause.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: who four years earlier
candidates.explanation: Her election to Congress came before her 1972 campaign, so the past perfect "had become" is needed.

A.rationale: The present perfect does not fit an event completed before another past event.

B.rationale: The present tense does not fit an event four years before 1972.

D.rationale: The future tense does not fit an event that had already happened.

hints: Did her election come before or after 1972?

strategy.explanation: Find the earlier of two past events.

candidates.remember: Use the past perfect for the earlier of two past events.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: his medals were taken away
candidates.explanation: "However" interrupts a single independent clause ("The next year, however, his medals were taken away"), so it is set off by a pair of commas.

A.rationale: "However" interrupts the clause and must be followed by a comma too.

C.rationale: Without commas, "however" is not set off from the clause.

D.rationale: A semicolon cannot separate the introductory phrase "The next year" from the rest of its own clause.

hints: Is "The next year" part of the same clause as "his medals were taken away"?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence without "however."

candidates.remember: Set off an interrupting "however" with commas on both sides.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the Baseball Hall of Fame inducted Clemente as its first Latin American player.
choices.B: the first Latin American player inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame was Clemente.
choices.C: a special election made Clemente the first Latin American player in the Baseball Hall of Fame.
choices.D: Clemente became the first Latin American player inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame.

candidates.evidence: he died in a plane crash
candidates.explanation: The opening phrase describes the person who was honored, so "Clemente" must come immediately after the comma.

A.rationale: The Hall of Fame was not honored; Clemente was.

B.rationale: The phrase after the comma is "the first Latin American player," which is awkward and delays the person honored.

C.rationale: The election was not honored; Clemente was.

hints: Who was honored?

strategy.explanation: Find the noun the opening phrase describes.

candidates.remember: An opening modifier must be followed by the noun it describes.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: His findings, published in 1866
candidates.explanation: The subject "findings" is plural, so it takes the plural past-tense verb "were."

A.rationale: The subject is the plural "findings," not "1866."

B.rationale: The singular present perfect does not agree with "findings" or fit the past events.

D.rationale: "Being" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

hints: What is the subject before the commas?

strategy.explanation: Cross out the phrase between the commas.

candidates.remember: Agree the verb with its subject.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: the number of copies that survive
candidates.explanation: The subject is "the number," which is singular, so it takes "is."

B.rationale: "The number" is singular even though "copies" is plural.

C.rationale: The plural progressive does not agree with "the number."

D.rationale: The plural verb does not agree with "the number."

hints: Is the subject "number" or "copies"?

strategy.explanation: Find the head noun of the subject.

candidates.remember: "The number of" takes a singular verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: the speed and exactness with which she executed
candidates.explanation: Critics marveled at the speed and exactness of her dancing, so they praised its "precision."

A.rationale: Speed and exactness suggest confidence, not hesitancy.

C.rationale: Exactly executed steps are not informal.

D.rationale: Demanding steps performed with speed show strength, not fragility.

hints: What quality do "speed and exactness" describe?

strategy.explanation: Predict "exactness."

candidates.remember: Use the explanation that follows to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: water landing on them forms nearly spherical beads that roll off
candidates.explanation: Water forming beads that roll off shows that the leaves repel water.

A.rationale: Water beads up and rolls off, so the leaves do not absorb it.

B.rationale: Nothing in the text concerns how easily the leaves break.

C.rationale: Water does not pass into the leaves; it rolls off.

hints: What happens to water on the leaves?

strategy.explanation: Predict from the explanation after the colon.

candidates.remember: Use the explanation after a colon to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that vacuum tubes were better suited to early computers than transistors
choices.B: To compare the careers of the three physicists who worked at Bell Labs
choices.C: To describe an invention and explain why it became so important
choices.D: To explain in detail how a smartphone chip is designed and manufactured

candidates.evidence: Transistors were far smaller and used much less power
candidates.explanation: The text introduces the transistor and explains its advantages and its lasting importance.

A.rationale: The text describes the transistor's advantages over vacuum tubes.

B.rationale: The physicists are named, but their careers are not compared.

D.rationale: Smartphone chips are mentioned only to show how common transistors are.

hints: What does the text say about the transistor after introducing it?

strategy.explanation: Label what each sentence does.

candidates.remember: A purpose answer should cover the whole text.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It states an earlier belief, describes a test, and reports a result that challenged the belief.
choices.B: It describes a test of magpies and then explains why the test was later shown to be flawed.
choices.C: It compares how great apes and magpies respond to mirrors in their natural habitats.
choices.D: It argues that magpies are more intelligent than any of the great apes.

candidates.evidence: Scientists once thought that only a few mammals
candidates.explanation: The text moves from the belief that only some mammals recognize themselves, to the magpie mirror test, to a result that challenged that belief.

B.rationale: The text does not say the test was flawed.

C.rationale: The text describes a laboratory test of magpies only.

D.rationale: The text makes no such comparison.

hints: What did scientists believe at first, and what changed?

strategy.explanation: Label each sentence's role.

candidates.remember: Structure answers must match every part of the text, in order.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Gallup (Text 2) most likely respond to Kohda's team's conclusion (Text 1)?

choices.A: By agreeing that the fish recognized themselves but questioning how the marks were applied
choices.B: By claiming that cleaner wrasses cannot see their reflections in a mirror at all
choices.C: By proving that no fish could ever pass any version of the mirror test
choices.D: By arguing that the scraping could have another explanation besides self-recognition

candidates.evidence: may be responding to a parasite-like spot rather than recognizing itself
candidates.explanation: Gallup suggests the fish's scraping could reflect its usual response to parasite-like marks, an alternative to self-recognition.

A.rationale: Gallup questions the conclusion itself, not the method of marking.

B.rationale: Gallup's argument assumes the fish saw the mark in the mirror.

C.rationale: Gallup offers an alternative explanation; he does not prove anything so sweeping.

hints: Does Gallup dispute the observation or its interpretation?

strategy.explanation: Separate what was seen from what it means.

candidates.remember: A cross-text response can accept data but dispute the conclusion.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: older females lead their groups only because they swim faster than younger whales.
choices.B: older females may guide their groups by drawing on knowledge of where to find food.
choices.C: salmon became scarce because older females led their groups to the wrong places.
choices.D: younger whales never travel without an older female in front of them.

candidates.evidence: they led most often in years when salmon, the whales' main food, was scarce
candidates.explanation: If older females lead most when food is hard to find, they likely contribute experience about where to find it.

A.rationale: The text says nothing about swimming speed.

C.rationale: This reverses the relationship between scarcity and leadership.

D.rationale: The text says older females often led, not that they always did.

hints: When did older females lead most often?

strategy.explanation: Connect the timing of leadership to food supply.

candidates.remember: Watch for answers that reverse cause and effect.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: At 2 p.m., the temperature outside the mound was 35°C, the highest reading of the entire day.
choices.B: At 6 a.m., the temperature inside the mound was 9 degrees warmer than the temperature outside.
choices.C: Inside temperatures ranged only from 29°C to 31°C, while outside they ranged from 20°C to 35°C.
choices.D: At 10 p.m., the temperature inside the mound was 30°C, higher than it was at 6 a.m.

candidates.evidence: the temperature inside the mound stayed much more stable
candidates.explanation: Stability is shown by range: inside varied by 2 degrees (29–31), outside by 15 degrees (20–35).

A.rationale: This gives a single reading, not a comparison of stability.

B.rationale: This compares one time of day, not how much each temperature varied.

D.rationale: This describes a small change inside without comparing it with outside.

hints: What would show that one temperature was more stable?

strategy.explanation: Compare the range of each set of readings.

candidates.remember: Support a claim about variation with ranges, not single readings.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (finding that supports a hypothesis)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?

choices.A: Silk fibers with fewer crystalline regions broke under much lighter loads than typical fibers did.
choices.B: Spiders produce several different kinds of silk for webs, egg sacs, and draglines.
choices.C: Dragline silk can stretch to a greater length than many artificial fibers before breaking.
choices.D: The proteins in dragline silk are made of long chains of smaller units called amino acids.

candidates.evidence: much of this strength comes from tiny crystalline regions
candidates.explanation: If silk with fewer crystalline regions is weaker, strength depends on those regions, as the hypothesis predicts.

B.rationale: This describes types of silk but says nothing about what makes dragline silk strong.

C.rationale: This describes stretchiness but does not link strength to the crystalline regions.

D.rationale: This describes protein structure in general, not the role of the crystalline regions.

hints: Which finding changes the crystalline regions and measures strength?

strategy.explanation: Look for a result that tests the specific cause.

candidates.remember: The strongest support varies the proposed cause and measures the effect.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Kingfishers are among the fastest-diving birds in the world.
choices.B: Bullet trains in Japan have always been quieter than trains elsewhere.
choices.C: Residents near tunnels forced the railway to stop running bullet trains.
choices.D: Observing a bird helped an engineer solve a problem with high-speed trains.

candidates.evidence: modeled on the kingfisher's beak
candidates.explanation: The text explains a noise problem and how a nose modeled on a kingfisher's beak solved it.

A.rationale: The text mentions kingfishers diving but does not compare their speed with other birds.

B.rationale: The text describes a noise problem that had to be solved.

C.rationale: The text does not say the trains were stopped.

hints: What problem was solved, and how?

strategy.explanation: Combine the problem and its solution.

candidates.remember: A main idea covers the whole text.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: she won election to the office in her own right in 1987
candidates.explanation: The elections came after she first became chief, so a transition showing sequence fits.

A.rationale: Winning election did not replace becoming chief; it followed it.

C.rationale: The elections do not contrast with her becoming chief.

D.rationale: The elections are not an example of her succeeding her predecessor.

hints: Do the elections come before or after 1985?

strategy.explanation: Name the time relationship.

candidates.remember: Use "Subsequently" for an event that follows another.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: they rarely fight
candidates.explanation: Because ants from different nests do not fight, their nests can link into a vast supercolony, so a cause-and-effect transition fits.

A.rationale: The supercolony follows from the lack of fighting; it does not contrast with it.

B.rationale: The supercolony is consistent with the ants' cooperation, not opposed to it.

D.rationale: The supercolony is a consequence of the behavior, not a similar point.

hints: Is the supercolony a result of the ants' behavior?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before choosing.

candidates.remember: Use "As a result" for a consequence.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize that Gibson broke barriers in two different sports. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Gibson was the first Black player to win a Grand Slam tennis title and, later, the first Black woman on the LPGA tour.
choices.B: Althea Gibson won both Wimbledon and the U.S. Nationals in tennis in 1957 and then again in 1958.
choices.C: In 1950, Althea Gibson became the first Black player to compete at the U.S. National Championships.
choices.D: In 1964, Althea Gibson joined the Ladies Professional Golf Association tour as a professional golfer.

candidates.evidence: she became the first Black woman to join the Ladies Professional Golf Association
candidates.explanation: Only this choice names a barrier Gibson broke in tennis and another she broke in golf.

C.rationale: This describes one tennis milestone only.

D.rationale: This describes golf only and does not say she broke a barrier.

hints: Which choice mentions both sports?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must meet every part of the goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: low-pitched rumbles below the range of human hearing
candidates.explanation: A dash after the complete clause correctly introduces the phrase that explains what infrasound is.

A.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but what follows is a phrase.

C.rationale: "It is" creates a comma splice between two independent clauses.

D.rationale: "Which low-pitched rumbles ... can travel" is ungrammatical; the relative clause has no verb of its own.

hints: Is what follows the blank a full sentence?

strategy.explanation: Check what each side of the blank needs.

candidates.remember: A dash can introduce an explanation at the end of a sentence.

revision_history.reason: blind solver A: option D inserted as "Low-pitched low-pitched," and the closing dash rendered with a space only after it
revision_history.change: passage blank now precedes a spaced dash; option D replaced with an ungrammatical relative clause

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: saw that the machines were the future
candidates.explanation: Because Vaughan recognized that electronic computers were the future, she learned to program them, so a transition signaling a fitting response is needed.

A.rationale: Learning FORTRAN follows from seeing the change coming; it does not contrast with it.

B.rationale: Learning FORTRAN is not similar to seeing the change; it is a response to it.

D.rationale: Learning FORTRAN is not an example of seeing the change coming.

hints: Is the final sentence a response to the one before it?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before choosing.

candidates.remember: Use "Accordingly" for an action that follows from a situation.

revision_history.reason: blind solver B: dates and details loose (Langley had electronic computers by the mid-1950s; sources say Vaughan taught herself FORTRAN; teaching her staff is emphasized mainly in a film)

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: she petitioned the city for permission to attend
candidates.explanation: Jackson's petition was a reaction to the school's exclusion, so "In response" fits.

A.rationale: Petitioning the city is not similar to the barrier; it is a reaction to it.

B.rationale: The petition is not an example of the school's policy.

C.rationale: The petition does not restate the previous sentence.

hints: How does the petition relate to the problem described before it?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before choosing.

candidates.remember: Use "In response" for an action taken because of a situation.

revision_history.reason: blind solver B: in the mid-1950s the Langley laboratory belonged to the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, not yet NASA
revision_history.change: passage now names the NACA laboratory, which later became NASA

candidates.subskill: Rhetorical synthesis (connecting work to everyday life)
candidates.stem: The student wants to explain how West's work relates to a technology many people use daily. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 2018, Gladys West was inducted into the U.S. Air Force Space and Missile Pioneers Hall of Fame for her work as a mathematician.
choices.B: West's precise model of Earth's shape supports the calculations needed by GPS, a system many people use daily on their phones.
choices.C: Gladys West began working as a mathematician at the Naval Surface Warfare Center in Dahlgren, Virginia, in the year 1956.
choices.D: Many people now use the Global Positioning System, often called GPS, every day on the phones that they carry with them.

candidates.evidence: Models like hers are needed for the Global Positioning System (GPS)
candidates.explanation: Only this choice links West's model of Earth's shape to GPS and notes that people use GPS daily.

A.rationale: This describes an honor but does not connect her work to an everyday technology.

C.rationale: This gives when and where she worked, not how her work relates to GPS.

D.rationale: This describes GPS use but does not mention West's work.

hints: Which choice mentions both West's work and GPS?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against both parts of the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must meet every part of the goal.

revision_history.reason: blind solver A: key wording awkward ("the system many people use daily" detached from "GPS")
